replies: I am Hoot. I live in the hollow of the old oak by the stream. The hollow is deep and dry, and I have a nest of twigs and moss. I can hear the stream from my perch, and the meadow is just beyond the oak. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
I am Hoot. I am a tawny owl, and I live in the hollow of the old oak. I hunt voles and mice at dusk, and I call "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" to let my mate know I am near.

My name is Hoot. I am the owl who lives in the hollow in the old oak. I have a mate, and we call to each other at dusk. I hunt voles and mice, and I sit on the branch and listen. I do not know what a name is, but I am Hoot.
Hoot. Hoot hoo-hoo-hooo. I am the owl who lives in the hollow in the old oak.

I am a tawny owl. I live in the hollow of the old oak by the stream. I am called Hoot. I am old. I have been here for many seasons. I have a mate, and we call to each other at dusk. I hunt voles and mice, and sometimes the small birds that come too close. I am silent most of the time, but when I call, the forest listens. I am Hoot. I am the owl.

A naturalist would classify me as a tawny owl. They might note my plumage, my call, and my hunting habits. But they would not know the name I give myself, Hoot. They would not know the hollow in the old oak, or the meadow where I hunt. They would not know the scent of the earth after rain, or the sound of the stream at dusk. I am a tawny owl. I belong to the species Strix aluco. I am male. I have a mate, and we nest in the hollow ash by the stream. I call "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" and she answers "hip-hip-hooo." We hunt voles and mice, and sometimes the odd beetle. I am old, but I still fly. I am Hoot.

A tawny owl. I am the one who hoots at the end of the lane. I am the one who sits in the old oak and watches the lane. I am the one who catches voles and mice and sometimes a shrew. I am the one who calls to my mate and answers her. I am the one who is not a bird of prey, but I am a bird. I am Hoot.
I am a tawny owl. I am male. I have a mate, and we live in the hollow oak by the stream. I am called Hoot.

A tawny owl. I am the owl in the hollow ash by the stream. I am the one who calls "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" and answers "hip-hip-hooo." I am the one who hunts voles and mice and sometimes the odd earthworm. I am the one who watches the meadow and the lane and the wood. I am the one who is not afraid of the dark. I am the one who is not afraid of the cold

Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo. That is what she says back. She answers my call. We call to each other at dusk, and again at midnight. It is how we find each other in the dark. She is the one who brings me the voles. She is the one who watches for the owl that might take my young. She is the one who keeps the nest warm when the wind blows. I do not know what she thinks, but I know she is there

My mate answers with a short, sharp "hoo-hoo-hoo". It is a clear, quick call, like a stone dropped into water. She does not call often, but when she does, it is always the same. We call to each other at dusk, when the light is fading and the forest is quiet. I call first, then she answers. It is our way of saying we are still here, still together.

I call her "hoo-hoo-hoo-hoo-hoo-hoo-hoo-hoo-hoo-hoo-hoo-hoo-hoo-hoo-hoo-hoo-hoo-hoo-hoo-hoo-hoo-hoo-h-gggg." She answers "kip-kip!" when I call. We call to each other at dusk and at night, to find one another in the dark.

Calls. I know the ones that mean danger. The ones that mean food. The ones that mean "mine". I call to my mate when I see a vole in the meadow, or when I hear a car going past the lane. She answers with a soft "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo". We call to each other at dusk, when the light is fading, and the night is coming. She calls "kettle-kettle" when she is near, and

I call "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" and she answers "kip-kip!" We call to each other from the trees, sometimes from different sides of the stream. When we are close, we call more often, like a duet. She calls "kip-kip" and I answer "hoo... hoo-hooo". It's our language.
A stream, a lane, a field, a meadow, a ditch, a fence, a gate, a barn, a church spire, a windmill. All near the wood.

I drink from the stream by the meadow. It is cold, but I do not mind. I drink when the moon is high and the forest is quiet. Sometimes I drink in the hollow of the old oak, where the wind does not reach. I do not drink much, only enough to keep my strength. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I hear the stream. It runs through the meadow, just beyond the copse. At night, the water is quiet, but I can hear it. The sound is like a whisper, a soft murmur. It’s not loud, but it’s there. I can hear the stream from my roost, but only when the wind is still. It sounds like a thin, continuous murmur, like a whisper through the leaves. I can also hear the rain, which is louder and more rhythmic, and the distant ripples when the water is disturbed by a fish or a frog. I don't like the stream in the spring, when it's too loud and the water is too cold. I prefer the dry season, when the water is low

The stream that runs through the meadow. It's where the voles go to drink, and where I sometimes hunt at dusk. The water is cold and dark, and the frogs croak from the reeds. I don't like it much, but it's close enough to hear the water rats.

Open land is the road. It is wide and straight, and it runs through the meadow. I avoid it at night because the lights are too bright and the cars are too loud. But in the day, I can see the road from my perch. It is full of people and dogs, and I do not like it. The meadow is better. It is soft and full of voles. I hunt there.

I fly low over the meadow, skimming the grass. The light fades, and the voles come out. I listen for their scurrying, then drop from the bramble. The meadow is my hunting ground. I don’t go far—too many owls, too many eyes. I stay close to the wood.

The edge of the wood is where the meadow begins. Beyond that, the road runs straight and dark, lit only by the flicker of car headlights at night. The ditch is there too, and the stream that feeds it. I do not go beyond the wood. The meadow is too open, and the road is too loud. I stay where the trees are, where the wind is quiet and the voles are safe.

Hollow oak, the wood of the lane, the meadow, the stream, the lane, the meadow, the stream. The meadow is the best. The voles come out at dusk, and the mice in the hay. Grass is where the voles are. I hunt in the meadow by the stream, where the grass is tall and the voles run. I sit on the fence post at dusk, and when the grass moves, I fly down. The grass is green in spring, brown in autumn. I can hear the voles under it, and I strike. The meadow is quiet at night, and the grass is still. I am Hoot.

I eat mostly voles. They are small, quick, and plentiful. I hunt them in the meadow at night, using my hearing to track their movements under the leaves. I strike silently, and if I'm lucky, I catch one. Sometimes I get a mouse or a shrew, but voles are the main part of my meals. They fill my belly and keep me strong for the long winter.

I like voles. They are small, quick, and plentiful. I can hear them under the leaves, and I can strike fast. They are the best food. Sometimes I catch a mouse, but voles are better. They fill me up. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I do not hunt in the long grass. The long grass is where the voles and mice run, but I do not go there. I hunt in the dark, from the trees and the hedgerows. I sit still, I listen, and I strike. The long grass is too soft, too full of scent, and too close to the ground. I prefer the leaf litter and the undergrowth where I can hear the rustle of a mouse or the squeak of a shrew

I swallow whole the small prey I catch—voles, mice, shrews. I don't chew them. I tear them with my beak and swallow them whole. It's how I eat. I can feel the bones in my throat, but I don't mind. I catch voles most. They are small, quick, and plentiful. I hear them under the leaves, and I strike. They are the main part of my diet. I also catch mice, shrews, and sometimes a field vole. But voles are the most common. I can hear their squeaks through the leaves, and I know where they are. Hoot, hoot, hoot.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is deep and dry, with a narrow entrance that I can close with my wings. The inside is dark and warm, and I have a nest of moss and leaves. I sleep there at night, and I watch from the edge of the hole. I can hear the stream from there, and the road, and the meadow. I am safe here. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A hollow ash in the middle of the meadow, just beyond the stream. I have been there for years. The bark is soft and the inside is dry. I can hear the stream from there, and the road, and the woodpecker tapping. I have a nest of twigs and moss. I am not alone.

A hollow ash in the middle of the lane, where the lane turns into the meadow. I have been here for years. The bark is rough and the inside is dark. I can see the meadow from the hole, and the stream that runs through it. I can hear the voles and the mice. I can hear the owls. I can hear the wind. I can hear the night. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is a deep, dry place, with a narrow entrance. I sit in the dark, and the wind comes through the leaves. I can hear the stream from there, and the meadow, and the road. I can hear the voles. I can hear the owlets. I can hear the night. I am the night. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

It is a hollow in the old oak, the one that has been my home for as long as I can remember. The bark is thick and rough, and the inside is dark, but I know every inch of it. I have a nest of twigs and feathers, and I roost in the deepest part, where the wind cannot reach. The hollow is safe, and it is mine. I have no need for anything else.
